content.text: It is time to write your very first C++ program! We will build a small program that prints a greeting on the screen. To do this, we need to understand the basic skeleton (called boilerplate code) that every C++ file uses.
1. Why do we need Boilerplate code?

Boilerplate code is like the foundation of a house. Before you can put up walls or paint the rooms, you need a solid base. In C++, the boilerplate setup tells the compiler where to import tools and where the program should start reading.

5. The Mega Header: bits/stdc++.h

Usually, in C++, you have to import different headers (like `<iostream>` for printing, `<string>` for text, or `<cmath>` for math) depending on what features you want to use. This means you might end up writing a lot of include statements at the top of your file.
Let us compare how your program changes when you write each header manually versus using the mega header side-by-side:
While bits/stdc++.h is great for saving time in speed coding contests, it makes compiling a bit slower because it imports everything. Avoid using it in real-world professional projects!
6. Visualize Execution Flow

steps.explanation:
The program begins by processing headers.

`#include <iostream>` imports the standard C++ library that lets us print output to the screen.

The CPU enters the `main()` function.

Every C++ program MUST have a `main()` function. This is the entry point where execution officially starts.

The print statement executes.

`std::cout` sends the text "Hello, World!" to the console screen. `std::endl` moves the screen cursor to the next line.

The program executes `return 0;`.

This tells the operating system that our code finished successfully without any issues. The program now terminates.

content.text: 7. Key Takeaways

· Main Function: Every C++ program must contain exactly one 'int main()' function as the entry door.
· Semicolons (;): Every instruction statement inside C++ must end with a semicolon, like a period at the end of a sentence.
· Mega Header: bits/stdc++.h imports all libraries in one line, but it slows down compile times.
8. Common Mistakes

· Missing Semicolon: Writing 'std::cout << "Hello"' without a ';' at the end. This is the most common C++ error!
· Case Errors: Writing 'Main()' instead of 'main()'. C++ is case-sensitive, so it won't find the entry point!
9. Practice Questions

content.question: What is the primary function of the '#include <iostream>' statement?
options: It declares the main entry function of the script.
It imports the library needed to print output text and read user keyboard inputs.
It sets the compiler's execution speed limit.

content.question: What happens if you omit the semicolon ';' at the end of an instruction statement in C++?
options: The compiler completes it automatically at runtime.
The compiler throws a syntax compilation error and refuses to build the code.
The editor converts the line into a comment.

What is the main benefit of using the mega header '<bits/stdc++.h>'?
options: It runs the code faster on the computer CPU.

content.text: 10. Summary

Boilerplate code lays the foundation for your C++ script. With library imports, main doors, print streams, and return codes, you have a solid scaffold. Now let us explore how to write notes to ourselves using comments!
